Worrell, E., Corsten, M. and Galitsky, C. (2015). Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for Petroleum Refineries: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers. Document Number 430-R-15-002, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, ENERGY STAR, February 2015. No DOI or URL printed.

Locators are printed page numbers (PDF page = printed + 5). An ENERGY STAR measure catalogue; almost every number is reprinted from other sources. Main file: (1) Table 3, the authors' estimated 2011 U.S. refinery energy balance, loaded per process unit as final fuel, steam and electricity intensities derived from the printed annual totals divided by the printed throughput (MMBtu/bbl and kWh/bbl of unit feed; hydrogen per lb, sulfur per short ton), with the formula; plus a combined CDU+VDU row per bbl of crude for distillation-column_atmospheric-vacuum (duplicates the separate CDU and VDU rows). Steam is steam energy content, not boiler fuel; negative steam = net export (thermal cracking, sulfur). Table 3 final/primary columns not loaded. (2) Whole technologies with their own numbers: desalter electricity, fired heater efficiency (75-90%; 82% -> 92% with air preheat), progressive crude distillation capex (2000$), hydrocracker power recovery turbine (910 kW, 1993$), refinery CHP ($1,000-2,500/kW; Baytown 73% CHP efficiency; Whiting 525 MW), Corus gas expansion turbine (2 MW, $2.6 million, O&M $110,000/yr), micro back-pressure steam turbine ($900/kW at 150 kW, <$200/kW at 2 MW, 20 yr), gas turbine pre-coupled to SMR ($700/kW), high-temperature CHP (incremental $630/kW), residue gasification and IGCC (Marano 2003; Domenichini and Mancuso 2008), CO2 capture abatement costs per t CO2 avoided (Ch. 20), slurry-phase hydrocracking state of development. Flows: hydrocracker hydrogen consumption (Nm3/bbl feed). _measures.csv: quantified measures of Chapters 6-19 with saving, cost and payback as printed. _other-values.csv: sector statistics, Table 3 assumptions (boiler 77%, cogeneration 32%, grid 32%) and totals, plant capacities without costs, capture-source shares. Not loaded: figures read only from charts (Figs. 1-12), water management (Ch. 21), qualitative innovative technologies (improved delayed coking, membranes, biodesulfurization, alternative desulfurization), energy management guidance and appendices.

(1) No price year for almost all costs (CHP, expansion turbines, gasification, CCS, measure costs): 2015 used per the rule; only progressive distillation (2000$), Zeeland turbine (1993$), Kemira (1991$) carry a year. (2) BP Whiting CHP cost printed as $250 million (p.92) and about $210 million (p.94). (3) Kemira standby boiler savings '54 TBtu/year' (p.47) and Petro-Canada Edmonton 'around 18 TBtu annually' (p.39) are implausible unit slips. (4) Chevron flare pilot '1.68 million scf/year (168 MMBtu/year)' is about 10x low (p.101). (5) Hydrocracker pressure '8.3 to 13.8 Bar' (p.15) is likely 83-138 bar. (6) Abstract says energy fell from 50% to about 30% of cash operating costs; introduction says expenditures fell by about 20%. (7) Table 6 prints 1% fuel saved for flue gas heat recovery while the text gives 2-4% (economizer) and 5-8% (condensing). (8) Table 3 'Fuel' for hydrogen (45,000 Btu/lb) is below the H2 heating value: feedstock gas probably excluded, not stated. (9) Heating-value basis not stated except heater maximum (92% HHV) and IGCC efficiencies (LHV). (10) Gasification capacities in 'tons per day' (short tons assumed). (11) CCS costs for the Shell study printed in USD with the original EUR 90-120 in parentheses; USD loaded. (12) Typos: 'Sanassazzo', 'Teroso', 'Krotz Sprinds', 'Fling J'.
